question: Which type of trailer is most at risk of getting stuck on a raised railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: A fully loaded tandem-axle van trailer
choice_b: A tanker hauling food-grade liquid
choice_c: A flatbed carrying steel coils
choice_d: A low-slung unit such as a lowboy, car carrier, moving van, or possum-belly livestock trailer
explanation: The manual specifically warns that low slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer) and single-axle tractors pulling long trailers set for a tandem-axle tractor can get stuck on raised railroad crossings.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.4 Railroad-highway Crossings

question: A "trailer jackknife" happens when:
choice_a: The wheels of the trailer lock up and the trailer swings around
choice_b: The trailer's landing gear collapses while underway
choice_c: The fifth wheel disengages from the kingpin
choice_d: The tractor's drive wheels lock up and the tractor swings around
explanation: The manual states that when the wheels of a trailer lock up, the trailer will tend to swing around -- this type of jackknife is often called a 'trailer jackknife.'
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: A trailer jackknife is more likely to happen when the trailer is:
choice_a: Empty or lightly loaded
choice_b: Fully loaded to legal maximum weight
choice_c: Carrying a liquid load with baffles
choice_d: Being towed at low speed on a straight highway
explanation: The manual states that trailer jackknife from wheel lock-up is more likely to happen when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_b: Feeling the steering wheel pull
choice_c: Hearing the tires squeal
choice_d: Waiting for the ABS light to flash
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize that the trailer has started to skid is by seeing it in your mirrors, and to check the mirrors any time you brake hard.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

topic: Combination Vehicles - Stopping a Trailer Skid
question: If your trailer starts to skid after hard braking, what should you do?
choice_a: Steer sharply toward the skid
choice_b: Release the brakes to get traction back
choice_c: Press harder on the foot brake
choice_d: Apply the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig
explanation: The manual instructs you to stop using the brake and release it to regain traction; using the trailer hand brake is wrong because trailer wheel braking is what caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.5 Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is "offtracking" (also called "cheating")?
choice_a: The trailer swinging out during hard braking
choice_b: The rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, tighter path than the front wheels when turning
choice_c: The trailer surging forward when liquid cargo shifts
choice_d: The tractor drifting sideways on wet pavement
explanation: The manual defines offtracking as the rear wheels following a different path than the front wheels when a vehicle goes around a corner, causing the path followed to be wider than the rig itself.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: In a combination vehicle with more than one trailer, which wheels offtrack the most in a turn?
choice_a: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_b: The wheels of the converter dolly closest to the tractor
choice_c: The front steering wheels
choice_d: The rear wheels of the tractor
explanation: The manual explains that if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will offtrack the most.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: When turning a combination vehicle, why should you keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb rather than swinging wide to the left before the turn?
choice_a: It stops other drivers from passing you on the right
choice_b: It keeps the trailer brakes cooler
choice_c: It is required by Maine law for all turns
choice_d: It reduces fuel consumption
explanation: The manual states that keeping the rear of your vehicle close to the curb, and turning wide only as you complete the turn, will stop other drivers from passing you on the right.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.6 Turn Wide

topic: Combination Vehicles - Backing with a Trailer
question: When backing a trailer, how should you turn the top of the steering wheel to make the trailer go in the direction you want?
choice_a: In the opposite direction from the way you want the trailer to go
choice_b: In the same direction you want the trailer to go
choice_c: Keep the wheel straight and use the trailer hand brake to steer
choice_d: It does not matter as long as you back slowly
explanation: The manual states that when backing a trailer (unlike backing a car, straight truck, or bus) you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from the way you want the trailer to go.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

topic: Combination Vehicles - Backing with a Trailer
question: If you must back a trailer on a curved path, you should back toward:
choice_a: Whichever side has more overhead clearance
choice_b: The passenger's side, to keep the trailer visible in the right mirror
choice_c: The driver's side, so you can see
choice_d: Either side, as long as a spotter is present
explanation: The manual advises that if you must back on a curved path, you should back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: The trailer hand valve (trolley valve or Johnson bar) should be used:
choice_a: Only when parking on a hill
choice_b: Only to test the trailer brakes, not while driving
choice_c: Whenever the ABS light illuminates
choice_d: As the primary brake for every stop
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes and should not be used while driving because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand valve to set the parking brake?
choice_a: It is illegal in Maine to touch the hand valve while parked
choice_b: It automatically disables the tractor protection valve
choice_c: It will drain the tractor's primary air tank instantly
choice_d: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers without spring brakes
explanation: The manual warns never to use the hand valve for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers that don't have spring brakes; use the parking brakes instead.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: What is the purpose of the tractor protection valve?
choice_a: It prevents the trailer landing gear from being raised while moving
choice_b: It keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak
choice_c: It locks the fifth wheel jaws automatically
choice_d: It controls the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual explains that the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve

question: The tractor protection valve will close automatically when air pressure drops into approximately what range?
choice_a: 60 to 80 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi
choice_c: 100 to 120 psi
choice_d: 5 to 10 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve

topic: Combination Vehicles - Trailer Air Supply Control
question: On newer combination vehicles, the trailer air supply control is:
choice_a: A red eight-sided knob you push in to supply air and pull out to shut it off
choice_b: A foot pedal located next to the clutch
choice_c: A green round knob near the ignition switch
choice_d: A toggle switch on the dashboard labeled ABS
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as a red eight-sided knob; pushing it in supplies air to the trailer, and pulling it out shuts off air and applies the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.3 Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What is the purpose of the service air line on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It powers the landing gear crank
choice_b: It only operates the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: It carries air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand valve to apply the trailer brakes
choice_d: It supplies air only to charge the trailer air tanks
explanation: The manual states the service line (also called the control or signal line) carries air controlled by the foot brake or trailer hand brake, and is connected to relay valves that apply the trailer brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.4 Trailer Air Lines

question: What are the two purposes of the emergency air line on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It only signals the ABS computer
choice_b: It powers the trailer lights and the landing gear
choice_c: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes on the combination
choice_d: It is used solely to test the fifth wheel lock
explanation: The manual states the emergency line has two purposes: it supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and it controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.4 Trailer Air Lines

question: Emergency air lines are typically color-coded with which color to avoid confusing them with the service line?
choice_a: Black
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Red
choice_d: Yellow
explanation: The manual notes that emergency lines are often coded with red (red hose, red couplers) to distinguish them from the blue service line.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.4 Trailer Air Lines

question: When connecting glad hands (hose couplers), how should the couplers be positioned before joining them?
choice_a: Press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90-degree angle to each other, then turn to lock
choice_b: Align them parallel and slide them together
choice_c: Snap them straight together without twisting
choice_d: Heat the rubber seals before connecting
explanation: The manual instructs that when connecting glad hands, you press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90-degree angle to each other, and a turn of the glad hand will join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: If you cross the air lines when coupling (connect service to emergency and vice versa), what happens?
choice_a: The tractor protection valve automatically corrects the connection
choice_b: Nothing changes, since both lines carry identical air
choice_c: The ABS system disables itself as a safety measure
choice_d: Supply air goes to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so spring brakes may not release
explanation: The manual warns that crossing the air lines sends supply air to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What is the purpose of dummy (dead-end) couplers on a tractor?
choice_a: To increase air pressure in the service line
choice_b: To replace the tractor protection valve
choice_c: To prevent water and dirt from getting into the coupler and air lines when not connected to a trailer
choice_d: To allow the tractor to be driven without any trailer brakes at all
explanation: The manual states dummy couplers are used to keep water and dirt from getting into the coupler and air lines when the hoses are not connected to a trailer.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: Why is it important to drain the trailer air tanks regularly?
choice_a: It increases the ABS sensor accuracy
choice_b: Water and oil buildup in the tanks can keep the brakes from working correctly
choice_c: It is required only if the trailer lacks a tractor protection valve
choice_d: It reduces the weight of the trailer for legal load limits
explanation: The manual explains that letting water and oil build up in the air tanks may keep the brakes from working correctly, so each tank's drain valve should be opened every day.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.6 Trailer Air Tanks

question: When a trailer is set up to tow another trailer, how should the shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back of that trailer be positioned if another trailer IS being towed behind it?
choice_a: Closed
choice_b: Half-open to reduce pressure
choice_c: It does not matter as long as the tractor protection valve works
choice_d: Open
explanation: The manual states you must check that all shut-off valves are in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.7 Shut-off Valves

question: Which trailers, according to the manual, are not required to have spring brakes?
choice_a: Any trailer with an ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: All trailers manufactured after March 1, 1998
choice_c: Only tanker trailers hauling non-hazardous liquids
choice_d: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes; those trailers rely on emergency brakes powered by air stored in the trailer air tank instead.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.8 Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: Why must you use wheel chocks when parking a trailer that has no spring brakes?
choice_a: Because the tractor protection valve cannot be engaged without chocks
choice_b: Because chocks improve the trailer's antilock braking response
choice_c: Because the emergency brakes only hold as long as air pressure remains in the trailer air tank, and it will eventually leak away
choice_d: Because chocks are required by federal law on all trailers regardless of brake type
explanation: The manual explains that on trailers without spring brakes, the emergency brakes hold only as long as air pressure remains in the trailer air tank; eventually the air leaks away and there will be no brakes, so chocks are essential.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.2.8 Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: July 1, 2005
choice_b: March 1, 1990
choice_c: March 1, 1998
choice_d: January 1, 1975
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: What color is the ABS malfunction lamp on a trailer, and where is it located?
choice_a: Red, on the rear bumper
choice_b: Blue, on the dashboard only
choice_c: Green, on the right side mirror bracket
choice_d: Yellow, on the left side, front or rear corner
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: How does ABS change your normal braking capability on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It replaces the need for the foot brake entirely
choice_b: It does not decrease or increase normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up
choice_c: It significantly shortens stopping distance on every stop
choice_d: It allows you to follow more closely and drive faster
explanation: The manual explains ABS is an addition to your normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: If your combination vehicle's ABS malfunctions, what should you do?
choice_a: Stop immediately and refuse to move the vehicle under any circumstances
choice_b: Continue driving normally using your regular brakes, and get the system serviced soon
choice_c: Increase speed slightly to compensate for reduced control
choice_d: Disconnect the trailer since it can no longer be towed safely
explanation: The manual states that if your ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes; drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: When positioning the tractor to couple with a semitrailer, why should you never back under the trailer at an angle?
choice_a: You might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_b: It will automatically trigger the tractor protection valve
choice_c: It voids the trailer's ABS warranty
choice_d: It causes the glad hands to disconnect
explanation: The manual instructs to put the tractor directly in front of the trailer and never back under it at an angle, because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: During coupling, what problem occurs if the trailer height is set too low before backing the tractor under it?
choice_a: The tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose
choice_b: The landing gear will retract on its own
choice_c: The service line will overpressurize
choice_d: The kingpin will automatically lock without tractor movement
explanation: The manual explains that if the trailer is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose; if too high, it may not couple correctly.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After backing the tractor under the trailer and locking the trailer brakes, how do you check that the coupling is secure?
choice_a: Disconnect the electrical cord and check for sparking
choice_b: Immediately drive at highway speed and observe handling
choice_c: Release all air from the emergency line and listen for leaks
choice_d: Raise the landing gear slightly and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked
explanation: The manual's Step 11 instructs to raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When visually inspecting the coupling, what should you look for between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: A small gap of about one inch is normal and expected
choice_b: Grease should be visibly dripping from the gap
choice_c: The gap should widen slightly when the trailer is loaded
choice_d: There should be no visible space; if there is, something is wrong
explanation: The manual states you must make sure there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; if there is space, something is wrong and the trailer could come loose easily.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: Why should you never drive with the landing gear only part-way raised?
choice_a: It is only a fuel-efficiency issue, not a safety issue
choice_b: It may catch on railroad tracks or other obstacles
choice_c: It disables the tractor protection valve
choice_d: It automatically applies the trailer spring brakes
explanation: The manual warns never to drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things; raise it all the way.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When uncoupling a tractor-semitrailer, why should you chock the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or you're not sure?
choice_a: It is required before the fifth wheel release handle can be pulled
choice_b: It prevents the landing gear from being lowered too quickly
choice_c: It keeps the kingpin from rusting while parked
choice_d: Air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing the emergency brakes and allowing the trailer to move
explanation: The manual explains that without spring brakes, air could leak out of the trailer air tank and release the emergency brakes, so chocks are needed to keep the trailer from moving.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.2 Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After pulling the tractor partially clear of the trailer during uncoupling, why should you stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer?
choice_a: To prevent the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
choice_b: It is required so the ABS lamp can complete a self-test
choice_c: To allow the trailer brakes to reset automatically
choice_d: To keep the glad hands connected for one more test
explanation: The manual's Step 7 instructs stopping with the tractor frame under the trailer, which prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.4.2 Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When inspecting the lower fifth wheel of a combination vehicle, where should the locking jaws be positioned on the kingpin?
choice_a: Around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin
choice_b: It does not matter as long as the safety latch is engaged
choice_c: Around the head, not the shank, of the kingpin
choice_d: Resting loosely against the kingpin without contact
explanation: The manual's fifth wheel inspection checklist specifies checking that locking jaws are around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.5.1 Additional Things to Check During a Walkaround Inspection

question: During a combination vehicle brake check, how do you verify that air flows all the way to the last trailer?
choice_a: Open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer and listen for air escaping, showing the system is charged
choice_b: Check only the dashboard air pressure gauge
choice_c: Drive the vehicle and observe braking performance
choice_d: Disconnect the electrical cord and inspect the pins
explanation: The manual describes opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; hearing air escaping shows the entire system is charged.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.5.2 Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How do you test the tractor protection valve on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Simply look at the dashboard warning light for five seconds
choice_b: Disconnect the service line and observe the ABS lamp
choice_c: Pull the trailer at highway speed and check for drift
choice_d: Charge the air system, shut off the engine, then step on and off the brake pedal until the air supply control pops out at the specified pressure range
explanation: The manual describes charging the trailer air brake system, shutting off the engine, then stepping on and off the brake pedal several times; the trailer air supply control should pop out (go to emergency) when pressure falls into the specified range, usually 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.5.2 Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How can you test that the trailer service brakes are connected and working?
choice_a: Check that the landing gear crank turns freely
choice_b: With normal air pressure and parking brakes released, move forward slowly and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control, feeling for the brakes coming on
choice_c: Verify the ABS malfunction lamp is illuminated
choice_d: Turn off the engine and listen for a hissing sound from the cab only
explanation: The manual explains that to test trailer service brakes, you check for normal air pressure, release the parking brakes, move forward slowly, and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control -- you should feel the brakes come on.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 6, Combination Vehicles, 6.5.2 Combination Vehicle Brake Check
